https://news.sky.com/story/robey-warshaw.title: Robey Warshaw's low profile finds spotlight in George Osborne appointment
https://news.sky.com/story/robey-warshaw.subtitle: Sky's Ian King explains what George Osborne's new employer is all about and says he can expect big rewards at the firm.
https://news.sky.com/story/robey-warshaw.text:
They are, according to George Osborne, "the best of the best".
Robey Warshaw, the investment banking boutique the former chancellor is joining, may not be a household name.
However, to many of the UK's corporate chieftains, the firm's three founding members - Sir Simon Robey, Simon Warshaw and Philip Apostolides - provide vital counsel.
Their expertise has proved immensely lucrative.
According to the Financial Times, which first reported on Mr Osborne's appointment, the partnership - which employs just 13 people - has generated profits of £207m during the past seven years.
Even in the year to the end of March 2020, a disappointing one compared with the previous 12 months, the partnership reported a profit of £17.9m. Those were split between the three men, with Sir Simon reported to have received £10m. The previous year, he collected £27m.
These fabulous rewards have been earned by the trio making themselves indispensable to chief executives and company boards embarking on mergers, acquisitions and other corporate transactions.
Among those that Robey Warshaw has advised in recent years include Comcast, the US communications and media giant, on its £30bn takeover of Sky, the owner of Sky News, in 2018; London Stock Exchange Group, on its $27bn takeover of the data business Refinitiv; and Vodafone, on the merger of its Indian business with local player Idea Cellular.
Those contacts in the top echelons of business have been forged by the trio in deal-making that, combined, adds up to a century's worth of experience.
Sir Simon, who at 60 is the senior of the three, only became a banker by chance. Having won a choral scholarship at Magdalen College, Oxford, he was contemplating a career as an opera singer when, one evening, he was sticking up posters in a local hotel to advertise a performance. The hotel was hosting a 'milk round' recruitment event for Lazard, the investment bank, whose representatives piqued his interest.
Initially, he had hoped to combine banking and singing, telling the Evening Standard in 2013: "The hard worker in me sort of fell in love with mergers and acquisitions. I was a complete novice but I found I had a knack for it, which was quite unexpected.
"Of course the problem with my kind of job is you are very unreliable in the evenings so it doesn't really work alongside any sort of performing or extra-curricular life. Banking won."
Sir Simon, a father of three daughters, has nonetheless retained strong links with the arts, for example as chairman of the council of Aldeburgh Music, the prestigious music centre in Suffolk, and more recently as chairman of the Royal Opera House. An early mentor at Lazard was Sir Philip Hampton, who went on to become chairman of RBS, Sainsbury and GlaxoSmithKline.
An Arsenal season ticket-holder, who for more than 20 years lived in a spectacular Georgian townhouse on Highbury Place close to both the club's old and new grounds, Sir Simon joined Morgan Stanley in 1987. There, among his other mandates, he defended Marks & Spencer in 2004 against Sir Philip Green's unwanted takeover bid.
It was also at Morgan Stanley where Sir Simon first identified the opportunities of tapping Westminster and Whitehall for staff - something that will now benefit Mr Osborne.
Among those recruited to Morgan Stanley by Sir Simon included the late Lord Heywood, the former cabinet secretary and Jonathan Powell, the former chief of staff to Tony Blair when the latter was prime minister. In 2013, Sir Simon decided to strike out on his own, setting up his own advisory boutique with Sir Simon Robertson, previously a partner at Goldman Sachs and later chairman of Rolls-Royce.
The partnership, initially called Robertson Robey, was joined shortly afterwards by Mr Warshaw. The pair generated £10m worth of revenues during their first year but, shortly afterwards, Sir Simon Robertson departed.
Sir Simon Robey and Mr Warshaw immediately formed Robertson Robey and enjoyed early triumphs advising AstraZeneca in its successful defence from Pfizer's unwanted takeover approach in 2014 and BG Group during its £47bn takeover by Royal Dutch Shell. They also advised the brewer SAB Miller during its £71bn takeover by AB InBev, being credited with forcing the latter to raise its offer no fewer than four times.
Like Sir Simon, Mr Warshaw, 55, began his career at one of the UK's storied old merchant banks. On graduating in 1986, he joined SG Warburg, just before the City was transformed by Margaret Thatcher's 'big bang' reforms.
Over the next 27 years, as Warburg eventually became part of the Swiss bank UBS, he established himself as the City's top media and telecoms banker, advising Vodafone on many of its landmark deals. Mr Warshaw, too, knows the nexus between finance and politics well. One of the last deals on which he worked for UBS was the privatisation of Royal Mail.
The quietly-spoken Mr Warshaw, a Liverpool supporter, has business and deal-making in his blood. His father, Michael, led a management buy-out of the retailer Knobs & Knockers in 1977 and later floated the business on the stock market, before going on to net £20m from the turnaround and sale of the cosmetics company Molton Brown.
Mr Apostolides, 52, worked with Sir Simon at Morgan Stanley and joined when he set up on his own. He and his wife Charlotte have homes in Kensington, west London, and in Oxfordshire.
The trio's appointment of Mr Osborne has raised eyebrows even though the path from politics to corporate finance is becoming increasingly well-trodden.
The influential Lex column in the Financial Times noted: "Mr Osborne has the contacts to help get deals over the line. He also has the public profile to attract unhelpful attention to a previously low-profile business. Robey Warshaw is taking a calculated commercial risk."
The Reuters Breakingviews column added: "The 49-year-old is in many ways an odd hire for the advisory firm...Osborne has no experience advising chief executives on deal-making, and his hallmark economic policy of austerity is now widely regarded as a catastrophic misjudgment."
For the former chancellor, given the potential rewards on offer, the move appears much less of a risk.

https://news.sky.com/story/former-chance.title: Former chancellor George Osborne leaves Evening Standard and Blackrock to join consultants Robey Warshaw
https://news.sky.com/story/former-chance.subtitle: Mr Osborne served as chancellor under David Cameron, before taking up editorship of the London Evening Standard.
https://news.sky.com/story/former-chance.text:
George Osborne has left his jobs at the London Evening Standard and Blackrock to join financial consultants Robey Warshaw.
The former chancellor of the exchequer served in David Cameron's cabinet starting in 2010, before leaving politics after Theresa May took power in 2016.
He is currently editor-in-chief at the Evening Standard, having previously served as editor.
At the end of March he will step down from this role, as well as his position as a senior adviser at investment firm Blackrock.
Mr Osborne has been known to hold as many as nine jobs at once. It is not clear if he will be leaving his other appointments ahead of his move.
Robey Warshaw was founded in 2013, and in a statement the company said the former Conservative MP would "significantly enhance the advice we give to clients".
Mr Osborne said he was proud to be joining an outfit he described as "the best of the best".
A spokesperson for Robey Warshaw said: "We founded Robey Warshaw eight years ago to help our clients to the very best of our collective abilities and we remain single-mindedly committed to that purpose.
"We believe that George will significantly enhance the advice we give to clients. He brings differentiated experience and expertise to our team from his leading roles in global finance over the past decade.
"We remain hugely ambitious about our company's future and believe that George will help expand our reach and what we can offer our clients without changing the philosophy or ethos of our firm."
Mr Osborne was first elected to Parliament in 2001 as an MP for Tatton in Cheshire, and stood down at the 2017 election.
That year he joined the Standard and Blackrock.
Mr Osborne said: "Robey Warshaw is the best of the best, advising great businesses on how to grow, and I'm proud to be joining this first-rate team."
